props.title: The Comb
props.initialSlug: Surreal puppet animation explores dream-logic mystery

sections.content: **The Comb (1990)** (1990) stands as one of the Quay Brothers' most haunting stop-motion masterpieces, diving deep into surrealist dream logic and psychological horror. Like their seminal Street of Crocodiles (1986), the film blends intricate puppet animation with unsettling mechanical movements. The brothers draw clear inspiration from **The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari** (1920), particularly in their use of sharp angles and expressionist shadows to create a nightmarish landscape that shifts between a sleeping woman's bedroom and a twisted dreamworld.

sections.content: The film's innovative mixing of live-action and animation creates a hypnotic meditation on dreams and desire. The sleeping woman's twitching fingers mirror the mechanical movements of the puppet world, suggesting an intimate connection between dreamer and dream. This technique influenced later experimental animators like **Priit Pärn** in **1895** (1995) and can be seen echoed in the dream sequences of **Paprika** (2006).

The titular comb becomes a powerful symbol of transition between states of consciousness, similar to the spinning top in **Inception** (2010) but employed with far more surrealist flair. The Quay Brothers' signature use of found objects and mechanized movements creates an atmosphere that feels both antiquated and timeless, drawing from Eastern European animation traditions while establishing their own unique visual language. sections.content: The film's influence extends beyond experimental animation into mainstream surrealist cinema. Directors like **Charlie Kaufman** in **Anomalisa** (2015) and **Henry Selick** in **Coraline** (2009) have cited the Quay Brothers' work as inspiration for their own explorations of dream logic and psychological spaces. The intricate puppet design and mechanical movements in **The Comb** (1990) particularly influenced the aesthetic of **Madame Tutli-Putli** (2007).
